interactions.label: A platelet adheres to exposed collagen at a wound site via von Willebrand factor

params.question: A platelet adheres to exposed collagen at a wound site via von Willebrand factor. If the platelet's glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors were non-functional, which step of primary haemostasis would fail?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasoconstriction is driven by endothelin-1 and neurogenic reflexes, not by platelet surface receptors.
Platelet adhesion is mediated by glycoprotein Ib binding to von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen. GPIIb/IIIa is not involved in adhesion.
Platelet activation is triggered by the adhesion step (via GPIb) and amplified by ADP and thromboxane A2. It does not require functional GPIIb/IIIa.
Correct. GPIIb/IIIa cross-links adjacent platelets using fibrinogen as a bridge. Its absence blocks aggregation — the molecular defect in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

overallFeedback.feedback: GPIb mediates adhesion (to collagen via vWF); GPIIb/IIIa mediates aggregation (linking platelets via fibrinogen). These two receptors correspond to two distinct steps of primary haemostasis.
GPIIb/IIIa is the aggregation receptor. Its deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where platelets adhere normally but cannot aggregate.

interactions.label: Why is heparin bridging mandatory when initiating warfarin therapy?

params.question: Why is heparin bridging mandatory when initiating warfarin therapy?

answers.text: Warfarin cannot suppress thrombin directly, so heparin is needed to inhibit thrombin until warfarin takes effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While warfarin does not directly inhibit thrombin, the reason for bridging is the differential half-lives of vitamin K-dependent proteins, not a gap in thrombin suppression.

answers.text: Protein C, an anticoagulant with the shortest half-life, is depleted before procoagulant factors, creating a transient pro-thrombotic state

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Protein C has a shorter half-life than procoagulant factors II, IX, and X. Warfarin depletes protein C first, temporarily removing anticoagulant protection before full anticoagulation is achieved.

answers.text: Warfarin cannot inhibit factor VII for the first 48 hours of therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In fact, factor VII has the shortest half-life among procoagulant factors and is depleted early. The issue is that anticoagulant protein C is depleted even faster.

answers.text: Heparin is needed to prevent warfarin-induced thrombocytopenia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warfarin does not cause thrombocytopenia. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is a separate entity caused by heparin itself, not warfarin.

overallFeedback.feedback: Warfarin depletes all vitamin K-dependent proteins, but protein C (anticoagulant) falls first due to its short half-life. This creates a brief pro-thrombotic state that heparin must cover.
Protein C's short half-life means it is depleted before procoagulant factors, creating a dangerous pro-thrombotic window that heparin covers until full anticoagulation is established.

interactions.label: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, microthrombi form throughout the vascula

params.question: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, microthrombi form throughout the vasculature yet the PT and aPTT remain normal. Which mechanism best explains this?

answers.text: Clotting factors are consumed but rapidly replenished by the liver

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: If the coagulation cascade were driving clot formation, factors would be consumed and PT/aPTT would prolong, as seen in DIC. TTP does not consume clotting factors.

answers.text: ADAMTS13 deficiency directly inhibits factors XII and VII, sparing the common pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ADAMTS13 is a metalloprotease that specifically cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers. It has no direct interaction with clotting factors.

answers.text: Microthrombi form through platelet aggregation around uncleaved vWF multimers, bypassing the coagulation cascade entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultra-large vWF multimers intact. These multimers spontaneously aggregate platelets in small vessels. Since the coagulation cascade is not activated, clotting factors are not consumed and PT/aPTT remain normal.

answers.text: Antithrombin neutralises any thrombin generated before it can prolong the screening tests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While antithrombin does regulate thrombin physiologically, this does not explain TTP. The microthrombi in TTP are platelet-driven, not thrombin-driven.

overallFeedback.feedback: In TTP, ADAMTS13 deficiency leads to uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers that aggregate platelets directly. Since the coagulation cascade is not involved, clotting factors are not consumed and PT/aPTT stay normal.
TTP is a disorder of platelet aggregation driven by uncleaved vWF multimers — the coagulation cascade is not activated, so PT and aPTT remain normal. This is the critical distinction from DIC.

interactions.label: A prolonged aPTT that corrects when mixed 1:1 with normal plasma indicates the p

params.question: A prolonged aPTT that corrects when mixed 1:1 with normal plasma indicates the presence of a factor inhibitor such as a lupus anticoagulant.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. Correction on mixing means the normal plasma supplied a missing factor — indicating a factor deficiency. Inhibitors such as lupus anticoagulant or anti-factor VIII antibodies neutralise the factor even when normal plasma is added, so the aPTT would NOT correct.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Correction on mixing indicates a factor deficiency, because the normal plasma supplies the missing factor. An inhibitor (anti-factor VIII antibody or lupus anticoagulant) would NOT correct on mixing, because it neutralises the factor even when normal plasma is added.

interactions.label: Both vitamin K deficiency and liver disease can prolong the PT. Which finding be

params.question: Both vitamin K deficiency and liver disease can prolong the PT. Which finding best distinguishes between them?

answers.text: D-dimer is elevated in liver disease but normal in vitamin K deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: D-dimer elevation is characteristic of DIC from secondary fibrinolysis, not of liver disease specifically. It does not reliably distinguish vitamin K deficiency from liver disease.

answers.text: Factor VIII is low in both conditions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Factor VIII is actually normal or elevated in both conditions. In liver disease, factor VIII remains normal because it is produced by endothelial cells, not hepatocytes. In vitamin K deficiency, factor VIII is unaffected because it is not vitamin K-dependent.

answers.text: PT corrects after intravenous vitamin K in deficiency but not in liver disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In vitamin K deficiency, hepatocytes are intact but lack the vitamin for gamma-carboxylation. Supplying vitamin K restores factor synthesis within 6–24 hours. In liver disease, damaged hepatocytes cannot synthesise factors regardless of vitamin K supply.

answers.text: Platelet count is always normal in liver disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Liver disease frequently causes thrombocytopenia through portal hypertension, splenic sequestration, and decreased thrombopoietin production.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is the response to intravenous vitamin K. In deficiency, intact hepatocytes resume gamma-carboxylation and PT corrects within 6–24 hours. In liver disease, damaged hepatocytes cannot synthesise factors regardless of vitamin K supply.
The vitamin K correction test is definitive: functional hepatocytes lacking vitamin K will resume factor synthesis when supplemented, while damaged hepatocytes in liver disease cannot respond.
